caption:
Lodge late? Here's what the ATO actually charges.

The 31 October deadline just passed. If you haven't lodged yet, here's the actual maths.

Failure to lodge (FTL) penalty: $364 per 28-day period (or part of one) your return is outstanding — capped at 5 periods, so a maximum of $1,820. The penalty unit rose from $330 to $364 on 1 July 2026, so this is higher than it was last year.

General Interest Charge (GIC): if you owe tax and don't pay by the due date, interest compounds daily on the outstanding amount. The longer you leave it, the more it grows.

If you're already late, the most important thing is to lodge — even if you can't pay the bill yet. The FTL penalty stops accumulating once you've lodged. The ATO penalises not lodging more heavily than not paying on time. Payment plans are available through the ATO's website.

A registered tax agent can apply for a lodgment extension on your behalf, and sometimes arrange remission of penalties — but they need to be on your behalf before you're penalised, not after.

Have you ever lodged late? What stopped you from lodging on time?

Narrated by an AI voice.

figures_checked: FTL penalty: $364 per 28-day period (or part), max 5 periods = $1,820 for individuals/small entities, 2026-27; penalty unit rose from $330 to $364 on 1 July 2026 (Kidmans Partners citing penalty unit legislation, checked 15 Nov 2026; ATO PS LA 2011/19 for FTL structure)
GIC applies on unpaid tax debt, compounds daily (ATO interest and penalties guidance, checked 15 Nov 2026)
